lessons.title: Tensors & basic operations in TensorFlow
objectives: Create and manipulate TensorFlow tensors
Explain how tensor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tensor with eager execution and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: TensorFlow tensors work much like PyTorch's or NumPy's arrays: multi-dimensional, typed, and shape-checked.
examples:
import tensorflow as tf
x = tf.constant([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
print(x.shape)             # (2, 2)
y = tf.matmul(x, x)        # eager execution -- runs immediately, prints real values
commonMistakes: Assuming TensorFlow still requires building an explicit static graph before running anything, as in TF1 — TF2's eager-by-default execution is deliberately much closer to normal.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing the eager-vs-graph distinction (even if you rarely touch graph mode directly today) explains a lot of TensorFlow's history and design in interviews.

lessons.title: Building a model with the Keras Sequential API
objectives: Define a simple model by stacking layers with the Sequential API
Explain how Sequential API changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Sequential API with layer stacking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Sequential API is the simplest way to build a model: a straight stack of layers, each feeding directly into the next, declared in order. It's fast to write and read, but only fits models with a single input, single output, and no branching or shared layers — for anything more complex, the Functional API (next lesson) is needed.
examples:
from tensorflow import keras
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu', input_shape=(784,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax'),
])
commonMistakes: Trying to force a model with multiple inputs or a skip-connection into the Sequential API — this API genuinely can't express that; recognize when you need the Functional API instead.
lessons.careerRelevance: Sequential models cover a large fraction of straightforward real tasks and are the fastest way to prototype an idea.
lessons.explain: The Sequential API is the simplest way to build a model: a straight stack of layers, each feeding directly into the next, declared in order. It's fast to write and read, but only fits models with a single input, single output, and no branching or shared layers — for anything more complex, the Functional API (next lesson) is needed.
lessons.example:
from tensorflow import keras
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu', input_shape=(784,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax'),
])

lessons.title: The Keras Functional API for flexible architectures
objectives: Build a model with multiple inputs, outputs, or branching using the Functional API
Explain how Functional API changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Functional API with multi-input/output models and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Functional API treats layers as callable functions applied to explicit tensor inputs, letting you build graphs Sequential can't express: multiple inputs, multiple outputs, or branches that merge back together (like a skip connection).
examples:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(784,))
x = keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(inputs)
outputs = keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)
commonMistakes: Defaulting to the Functional API's added complexity for a simple single-path model — Sequential is simpler and sufficient whenever your architecture genuinely has no branching.
lessons.careerRelevance: Real production architectures (multiple input types, auxiliary outputs) very often need the Functional API's flexibility, not just Sequential.
lessons.explain: The Functional API treats layers as callable functions applied to explicit tensor inputs, letting you build graphs Sequential can't express: multiple inputs, multiple outputs, or branches that merge back together (like a skip connection).

outputs = keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)

lessons.title: tf.data pipelines for real datasets
objectives: Build an efficient input pipeline with tf.data
Explain how tf.data.Dataset changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tf.data.Dataset with shuffle/batch/map/prefetch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: `tf.data.Dataset` builds an efficient, composable input pipeline: load data, apply transformations (shuffle, batch, map a preprocessing function, prefetch), and feed it to training — designed so data loading/preprocessing can overlap with GPU computation instead of blocking it, which matters a lot for real dataset sizes.
examples:
dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((images, labels))
dataset = dataset.shuffle(1000).batch(32).map(preprocess_fn).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
for batch_images, batch_labels in dataset: ...
commonMistakes: Loading and preprocessing an entire large dataset eagerly into memory up front instead of building a lazy tf.data pipeline — this doesn't scale to real dataset sizes and wastes the overlap.
lessons.careerRelevance: tf.data pipelines are the standard, expected way real TensorFlow training scales past toy-sized datasets.
lessons.explain: `tf.data.Dataset` builds an efficient, composable input pipeline: load data, apply transformations (shuffle, batch, map a preprocessing function, prefetch), and feed it to training — designed so data loading/preprocessing can overlap with GPU computation instead of blocking it, which matters a lot for real dataset sizes.
lessons.example:
dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((images, labels))
dataset = dataset.shuffle(1000).batch(32).map(preprocess_fn).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
for batch_images, batch_labels in dataset: ...

lessons.title: Training with model.fit and custom training loops
objectives: Train a Keras model with model.fit, and know when a custom training loop is needed instead
Explain how model.compile/fit changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model.compile/fit with tf.GradientTape and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: For standard cases, `model.compile()` (specifying optimizer, loss, metrics) followed by `model.fit()` handles the entire training loop for you — batching, gradient updates, validation, all in one call.
examples:
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
history = model.fit(train_dataset, validation_data=val_dataset, epochs=10)

# custom loop, when fit() isn't flexible enough:
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    predictions = model(x, training=True)
    loss = loss_fn(y, predictions)
grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))
commonMistakes: Reaching for a custom GradientTape loop by default 'for control' when model.fit() with callbacks would handle the case perfectly well — the built-in loop covers the large majority of real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing both the high-level (fit) and low-level (GradientTape) paths, and when each is appropriate, is a mark of real TensorFlow fluency.
lessons.explain: For standard cases, `model.compile()` (specifying optimizer, loss, metrics) followed by `model.fit()` handles the entire training loop for you — batching, gradient updates, validation, all in one call.
lessons.example:

# custom loop, when fit() isn't flexible enough:

    loss = loss_fn(y, predictions)
grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)

lessons.title: Debugging TensorFlow models
objectives: Apply a systematic checklist when a TensorFlow model isn't training correctly
Explain how shape debugging changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect shape debugging with overfit-small-subset test and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The same debugging discipline from the PyTorch track applies here: check shapes explicitly at each step, try to overfit a tiny subset of data first (if that fails, the bug is in your code), and inspect actual data batches rather than assuming preprocessing worked.
examples:
# same 'overfit 10 examples' test as PyTorch:
# if the model can't drive loss near zero on 10 examples, the bug is in your code
# (wrong loss, bad labels, frozen layers) -- not dataset difficulty or model capacity
commonMistakes: Assuming a non-learning model just needs more epochs or a bigger model before ruling out an actual bug with the fast small-subset overfit test.
lessons.careerRelevance: This debugging method transfers directly between PyTorch and TensorFlow, since the underlying causes of training bugs are largely framework-agnostic.
lessons.explain: The same debugging discipline from the PyTorch track applies here: check shapes explicitly at each step, try to overfit a tiny subset of data first (if that fails, the bug is in your code), and inspect actual data batches rather than assuming preprocessing worked.

lessons.title: Callbacks & training monitoring
objectives: Use Keras callbacks to monitor and control training automatically
Explain how EarlyStopping changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect EarlyStopping with ModelCheckpoint and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Callbacks hook into the training loop at specific points (end of each epoch, when a metric stops improving) without you writing manual loop logic: EarlyStopping halts training when validation loss stops improving (fighting overfitting automatically), ModelCheckpoint saves the best-performing version seen so far.
examples:
callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint('best_model.keras', save_best_only=True),
]
model.fit(train_dataset, validation_data=val_dataset, epochs=50, callbacks=callbacks)
commonMistakes: Manually watching a training log and stopping by hand when it looks like it's overfitting — EarlyStopping automates exactly this, more reliably and reproducibly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Using callbacks well is what separates a quick prototype training script from a robust, unattended training pipeline.
lessons.explain: Callbacks hook into the training loop at specific points (end of each epoch, when a metric stops improving) without you writing manual loop logic: EarlyStopping halts training when validation loss stops improving (fighting overfitting automatically), ModelCheckpoint saves the best-performing version seen so far.
lessons.example:
callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint('best_model.keras', save_best_only=True),
]
model.fit(train_dataset, validation_data=val_dataset, epochs=50, callbacks=callbacks)

lessons.title: Saving, exporting & deploying a TensorFlow model
objectives: Save a trained model and describe TensorFlow's deployment paths
Explain how model.save/load_model changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model.save/load_model with TensorFlow Serving and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: TensorFlow's native format saves the full model (architecture AND weights) in one step, simpler than PyTorch's weights-only convention.
examples:
model.save('my_model.keras')                       # full model: architecture + weights
loaded = keras.models.load_model('my_model.keras')   # ready to use immediately, no need to redefine the class

# deployment targets:
# TensorFlow Serving -> standard server API
# TensorFlow Lite    -> mobile/edge
# TensorFlow.js      -> in-browser
commonMistakes: Assuming every deployment target needs the same model format/optimizations — mobile (Lite) and browser (.js) deployment typically need additional conversion and often.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing which deployment path fits a given target (server, mobile, browser) is a practical, real architecture decision, not just a technical footnote.

lessons.title: Common TensorFlow/Keras pitfalls
objectives: Recognize frequent, specific TensorFlow mistakes
Explain how output activation mismatch changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect output activation mismatch with loss function mismatch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Forgetting to specify an output activation matching the task (e.g. softmax for multi-class, sigmoid for binary) causes subtly wrong training.
examples:
# common mismatch:
# labels are integers (0,1,2) but loss='categorical_crossentropy' expects
# one-hot vectors -- use 'sparse_categorical_crossentropy' for integer labels instead
commonMistakes: Using categorical_crossentropy with integer labels instead of one-hot vectors -- this either errors or silently trains incorrectly depending on the Keras version.
lessons.careerRelevance: These specific pitfalls account for a large share of real debugging time in TensorFlow/Keras projects.
